title: Inside the Muslim Manosphere Policing Women Online
gist: WIRED Middle East examines how a religiously branded strand of the manosphere, spread by creators like Kareem Atta’i and Ali Dawah, polices and harasses Muslim women online. An ISD analysis of about 14,000 Jordanian Instagram comments found 72 percent of abusive comments targeted women, while researchers lack platform data to show how recommendation systems drive the behavior.

insights.claim: The Muslim manosphere takes ideas circulating in the wider manosphere (feminism destabilized society, women hold too much power, men must reassert control) and rebrands them in the language of faith.
insights.speaker: Maysaa Ajjan
insights.so_what: Religious framing is a packaging layer on a global content genre, so the same demand and distribution dynamics apply across cultures.
insights.quote: It’s adopted those ideas circulating through the wider manosphere and rebranded them in the language of faith.

insights.claim: The article says it is debatable whether manosphere grievance is organic or engineered to sell supplements and other products.
insights.speaker: Maysaa Ajjan
insights.so_what: The monetization motive behind the content is left unresolved, so audience size alone does not show organic demand.
insights.quote: whether that’s entirely organic or engineered to sell supplements and other products is up for debate

insights.claim: Arabic manosphere creators adapt the ideology to local anxieties around religion, masculinity, marriage, money, and social change rather than just translating Western Red Pill content.
insights.speaker: Maysaa Ajjan
insights.so_what: Localization is what makes the content sticky, and it implies region-specific rather than imported demand.
insights.quote: The Arabic manosphere does more than translate Western Red Pill content.

insights.claim: Influencers build audiences by tapping financial insecurity, political instability, religious identity and fears of declining morality, turning misogyny into an explanation for broader frustration with women as its visible target.
insights.speaker: Sarah Kaddoura
insights.so_what: Economic and political stress is the audience funnel, so deteriorating conditions plausibly raise the addressable audience.
insights.quote: Misogyny becomes an explanation for a much wider sense of frustration—and women become its most visible target.
insights.locator: Kaddoura says influencers use financial insecurity

insights.claim: The author locates the problem in the use of real or claimed religious authority to legitimize misogyny, harassment and surveillance of women, not in religious expression online.
insights.speaker: Maysaa Ajjan
insights.so_what: Claimed authority makes disagreement look immoral, which blunts criticism and moderation pressure.
insights.locator: The problem is not religious expression online

insights.claim: Relationship coaches and preachers present personal opinions as religious instruction, so disagreement appears immoral and criticism can be cast as proof the creator is defending the faith against hostile forces.
insights.speaker: Sarah Kaddoura
insights.so_what: Criticism becomes fuel for the creator, which makes the content resistant to pushback.
insights.locator: That becomes even thornier when religion

themes.theme: Creators and the Dawah Bros lineage

insights.claim: Jordanian relationship coach Kareem Atta’i, who posts as Coach Kareem or Red Pill Arabic, packages his ideas as relationship advice while framing male-female interactions as power contests and describing violence as a means of disciplining women.
insights.speaker: Maysaa Ajjan
insights.so_what: Advice-style packaging gives violence-endorsing content a lower-friction entry point on platforms.
insights.locator: Atta’i packages his ideas as relationship advice

insights.claim: UK-based creator Ali Dawah, whose channel mixes street debates and commentary, is one of many so-called Dawah Bros who are generally more aggressive than inviting in promoting manosphere-style content.
insights.speaker: Maysaa Ajjan
insights.so_what: The phenomenon is cross-border and cross-language, so it is not a regional-only moderation problem.
insights.quote: The Muslim manosphere is also not confined to the Arab world.
insights.locator: Take prominent UK-based creator Ali Dawah

insights.claim: Kaddoura sees Dawah Bros as a platform-native successor to 1990s Egyptian and Saudi TV sheikhs, but they are unbounded by scheduled broadcasts and reach people who never chose to call in.
insights.speaker: Sarah Kaddoura
insights.so_what: Moving from scheduled broadcast to always-on feeds changes the reach of moral authority figures, which is a distribution shift more than a content shift.

insights.claim: A 2026 Institute for Strategic Dialogue report of nearly 14,000 Instagram comments aimed at 40 prominent Jordanian figures found 72 percent of hate, harassment or abusive comments targeted women.
insights.speaker: Maysaa Ajjan
insights.so_what: This is the main quantitative evidence in the piece, and it covers one platform in one country over 12 months.
insights.locator: A 2026 report by the Institute for Strategic Dialogue

insights.claim: Of Jordanian Instagram comments classed as religious or moral harassment (11 percent of the abusive set), 85 percent targeted female influencers.
insights.speaker: Maysaa Ajjan
insights.so_what: Moral policing is highly gendered in the data, which supports the claim that religious framing is directed at women.
insights.locator: A 2026 report by the Institute for Strategic Dialogue

insights.claim: All comments classified as sexual harassment in the ISD sample were directed at women, so the same environment that tells women to be invisible also subjects them to unwanted sexual attention.
insights.speaker: Maysaa Ajjan
insights.so_what: Moral policing and sexual harassment coexist, which the author reads as contradiction in how women are policed.
insights.locator: Additionally, all of the comments classified as sexual harassment

insights.claim: Mariam, admin of a roughly 400,000-member Facebook group for women in the UAE, disabled Facebook Messenger after unsolicited messages from men telling her how to dress and cover up, or sexually harassing her, or both.
insights.speaker: Maysaa Ajjan
insights.so_what: Prominent women withdraw from messaging channels, a cost borne by community managers and platform engagement.
insights.quote: They “either want to advise you to be holy and cover up, or they want to sexually harass you—or both.”

insights.claim: Kaddoura says a new account created as a male on TikTok, YouTube, X or Instagram is quickly served misogynistic content by the recommendation algorithm.
insights.speaker: Sarah Kaddoura
insights.so_what: Default feed behavior for new male accounts is a platform-design and regulatory exposure, though the claim is her assertion and not a measured result here.
insights.quote: it doesn’t take long for the algorithm to start recommending misogynistic content
insights.locator: The manosphere’s reach is shaped in part

insights.claim: Engagement-based systems can amplify emotionally charged and polarizing content, and content blaming women for men’s loneliness or financial insecurity draws reactions from supporters, critics and targets alike, which can raise its visibility.
insights.speaker: Maysaa Ajjan
insights.so_what: Outrage from critics also feeds distribution, so counter-speech can raise reach and ad-supported engagement models carry this incentive.

insights.claim: Researchers cannot see the internal platform data needed to trace how users move between creators and communities, so it remains unknown how passive exposure becomes active engagement or whether prolonged exposure changes behavior.
insights.speaker: Maysaa Ajjan
insights.so_what: The causal link between algorithms and harassment is unproven, and data access is the bottleneck for regulators and researchers.
insights.quote: limited access to the internal data needed to trace how users move between creators and communities
insights.locator: But how exactly a user’s behavior tips over

insights.claim: The author describes the harassment chain as a creator publishing a video, recommendation systems carrying it into feeds, and users repeating its message in women’s comments and inboxes on repeat.
insights.speaker: Maysaa Ajjan
insights.so_what: The chain places platform distribution between creator and harasser, which frames it as a product-level issue.
